title: The UAE Just Left OPEC After 60 Years. India Is Scrambling to Lock In the Best Energy Deal of a Generation.
excerpt: Abu Dhabi's exit from the oil cartel frees it to pump more crude — and New Delhi is positioning itself as the first major buyer in line. The stakes: $145 billion in annual oil imports and a strategic petroleum reserve that's only two-thirds full.
body:
On May 1, OPEC's third-largest producer walked out of the cartel it had helped define for six decades. The United Arab Emirates now pumps about 3.5 million barrels per day — roughly 4 per cent of global oil output — and it no longer answers to Vienna.

For India, which imports 85 per cent of its crude, the timing could not be more consequential. Brent crude sits at $111 a barrel, up roughly 76 per cent in a year, with the Strait of Hormuz functionally constrained by the US-Israel conflict with Iran. Every $10-per-barrel rise adds $13–14 billion to India's net oil import bill and shaves 0.3 per cent of GDP off the current account deficit. The Reserve Bank of India estimates a 15-basis-point drag on GDP growth for every 10 per cent rise above its baseline crude assumption.

## Why the UAE Left

Abu Dhabi's frustration had been building for years. The UAE spent a decade lifting its production capacity past 4.8 million barrels per day, only to be capped by quotas set largely in Riyadh. By 2027, it is targeting 5 million barrels per day — a goal flatly incompatible with cartel discipline.

Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei chose this moment because the price effect would be minimal, and so far that calculation has held: Brent rose less than 3 per cent on the news, with most of the movement pinned on Iran. But the structural damage to OPEC is real. The cartel's share of global oil output has already slipped from 48 per cent to 44 per cent, and without the UAE, the next Vienna communiqué will carry considerably less weight. Saudi Arabia will have to bear the burden of price stabilisation almost alone.

## India's Window

Freed of quotas, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) needs reliable, large-scale buyers for its incremental output. India's refining hubs at Jamnagar, Vadinar, and Paradip are natural candidates. The bilateral scaffolding is already deep: a 2022 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, a 10 per cent Indian stake in the Lower Zakum oilfield, and 5.86 million barrels of ADNOC crude already stored at India's Mangalore strategic reserve.

The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) adds another layer. When one of the corridor's anchor energy producers is selling outside a quota, the infrastructure becomes considerably more useful for both sides.

India's Ambassador to the UAE, Deepak Mittal, has been explicit about the opportunity. "The UAE's exit from OPEC opens new avenues to deepen our energy security cooperation," he said ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's May 15 visit, during which the two sides were expected to sign agreements on LPG supply and strategic petroleum reserves.

## The Strategic Reserve Gap

India's Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) was at 64 per cent capacity as of March 2026. The combined cover of 74 days still trails the International Energy Agency's 90-day benchmark — a gap that looks increasingly dangerous with Hormuz under pressure and Gulf producers routing 45–50 per cent of barrels through the strait.

Analysts at the Observer Research Foundation argue that two moves should follow immediately. First, a multi-year offtake from ADNOC at term pricing, with a slice of volume invoiced in rupees. Term contracts smooth the volatility that OPEC will no longer be able to dampen. Second, filling the SPR to capacity at current prices — a roughly $2 billion outlay that looks like modest insurance against a $145 billion annual import bill.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora invested in Indian equities, the OPEC fracture is a double-edged development. Lower long-term crude prices would be a structural positive for oil-marketing companies, airlines, and the broader consumer economy. But the transition period is volatile. Iraq, a chronic quota-buster, now has political cover to increase its own output, which could trigger a messy supply surge before markets stabilise.

The rupee is also in play. The Reserve Bank's ability to manage imported inflation depends on oil prices staying within its comfort zone — and with one of the cartel's key stabilisers now freelancing, that zone just got harder to define.

What is clear is that the 1970s oil-pricing architecture is unwinding in real time. What replaces it is transactional, bilateral, and more volatile. For India, the best defence is speed: lock in the contracts, fill the reserves, and deepen the Abu Dhabi relationship before the rest of Asia catches on.
